name: Fatima Lopez

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m a senior researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. We sell nothing and campaign for no side. Your answers are confidential. What happens on a normal shift?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I’m 43 and lead the Saturday calls and chats at the contact centre. My two-year college diploma opened the door, and years of tracing double charges made me one of the strongest agents here. The Saturday premium makes my pay higher than usual. I use AI now and then to sort a long case after another lead has checked the tool, but I verify each charge against the account.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What waits for you outside work?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner Ben repairs buses, and we have two children in school and a mortgage. We have about ten months of expenses saved, and there are plenty of other centres nearby. I like a call where a customer finally sees the corrected charge. I dislike a beautiful summary that hides a second debit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the Saturday desk AI Plateau looks like the sorter we already have, useful for finding a second debit but not deciding whether it is real. I would keep the original account open beside the summary.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think my Saturday pay is safe in this picture. Ten months saved gives Ben and me room for a repair, but I would not spend it because a screen saves five minutes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2026 I’d keep leading the Saturday queue and check each AI-sorted case against the account. In the first year of small change, I’d show two new agents the double-charge check during their paid shifts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm about the rota, attentive to customers. A tidy summary can still charge a family twice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which double charge would you teach?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last week the sorter merged two card payments into one line. I opened the ledger with a trainee and showed her that the second charge had a different date.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you use the savings?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ben (my partner) and I keep the savings for the mortgage and unexpected repairs. I would leave that account alone while the Saturday wage keeps coming.

I’d keep the **original account** beside every AI summary.
think: I think my **Saturday wage** remains safe here.
I would preserve the **ten-month reserve** for mortgage or repairs.
do: Keep leading **Saturday calls** and checking AI-sorted cases against accounts in 2026.
Coach **two new agents** through double-charge checks on their paid shifts in the first year.
feel: **Calm** about shifts, attentive to wrong charges.

fieldNote: She teaches from **dated payment lines**, not polished summaries.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say Steady Disruption may take the simple billing chats but leave costly wrong charges for people to fix. I would ask the centre to show paid Saturday hours beside any claim that the new system works.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think knowing the old sorter does not guarantee my premium when a stronger one arrives. Ten months saved gives me time to compare nearby jobs, but Ben’s repair wage cannot replace both incomes under the mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2026 I’d learn the new charge-checker by testing twenty old double debits on a paid shift if the manager allows us to log errors. In the first year routine chats move, I’d apply for a posted paid billing-review role only if written weekly pay and hours cover the mortgage and replace enough Saturday premium after travel; I’d keep my present paid rota until a signed offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about the premium, curious about the checker. A missing Saturday shift is a pay cut even if my title stays.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the test sheet count?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would count wrong dates and the repeat calls each wrong charge creates. If the checker misses a debit, the test sheet should show what a paid agent did next.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you compare a review role?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask Ben (my partner) to compare a full week’s wages and travel, not an hourly rate. Our children’s pickup still has to fit around that week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the team AGI by 2028 could settle a double-charge case from beginning to end before any of us checks the ledger. I would ask for posted paid jobs and the date our Saturday rota changes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think my lead wage could fall quickly in 2028, even though I use a small AI tool already. Robots around 2031 reach physical work later; ten months saved is a search window, not a permanent income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2026 I’d delay the planned patio roof while the existing cover is sound and keep its money in our existing house reserve. In the first year after 2028, I’d apply for a posted paid hospital-stores job only if written weekly wage and hours cover mortgage after travel and childcare; I’d take a paid trial if offered and leave the centre only after a signed offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about how fast the pay could change, but able to inspect a real shift. Ten months in the bank cannot make a lost Saturday premium grow back.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a stores trial show?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask for a full paid shift receiving and putting away supplies, not a walk past clean shelves. Robots may reach that work around 2031, so I would not sell it to Ben as permanent safety.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do about the patio roof?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ben (my partner) and I can mend the old cover instead of buying the new patio roof. We would keep the money available for the mortgage while I search.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say AGI by 2031 gives us time to see whether the hospital stores actually has paid openings. I would ask for a posted wage, not just an invitation to learn inventory words.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I can learn the stock work over five years, but robots around 2034 may later do it too. My current Saturday wage deserves a real replacement, not a hopeful certificate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: From 2026 I’d take an employer-funded stores-safety course on paid time only if a posted paid stores vacancy requires it, and try a paid stores shift if one is offered. In the first year after 2031, I’d move only on a signed offer showing written weekly wage and hours covering mortgage after travel and childcare; otherwise I’d keep paid calls.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, with time to test more than a course advert. I want to know what the loading bay pays before I leave the billing desk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What must the course include?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the trainer to let me check the cold-storage log and carry a crate safely. A lesson on a screen would not show me the weight of an actual delivery.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would pickup fit?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would compare the stores rota with Ben (my partner) around school pickup. If it ends after the children finish, paid care must fit inside the wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say AGI by 2036 gives us years to see which paid billing jobs remain and train new agents on the mistakes a tidy summary hides. I would ask each year for paid coaching hours, not merely a count of completed chats.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I could earn the Saturday premium for years and add to savings, yet full thinking AI may still take the billing desk in 2036. Robots around 2039 do not delay a screen-work change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2026 I’d keep leading Saturday calls and transfer a fixed part of each premium payment to our mortgage reserve. In the first year after 2036, if my paid hours fall, I’d move to a posted paid service-coach role only on a signed written offer showing weekly wage and hours that cover mortgage after travel and childcare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Watchful about the distant end, secure about this year’s shifts. A decade before AGI reaches my calls is time to teach and save while the paid rota is real.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you teach a new agent?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would teach a new agent to find the second debit in the ledger before closing a ticket. If the centre calls a video coaching, I would ask where the paid trainer is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you move the children?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep the children at their school unless Ben (my partner) and I had a signed offer and a manageable trip elsewhere. Plenty of centres nearby give me places to try first.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 troubles me most because it could do the double-charge check before I earn another Saturday premium. Ten months saved is a good search window, but our mortgage and school week still need a wage. I would need a posted paid alternative with written hours and pay covering the mortgage after travel and childcare, a paid trial, and a signed offer before leaving.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You did not ask whether a customer can challenge a correction made by a machine. My first trainer made me explain the second debit aloud before closing a case.

headlineQuote: My first trainer made me explain the second debit aloud before closing a case.
portrait: At **43**, Fatima is a highly skilled Saturday lead with a two-year diploma and higher premium pay.
She and Ben support **two schoolchildren** and a mortgage with ten months saved.
She uses **AI occasionally** but checks double charges against account records.
She tests **paid new work** while guarding the whole weekly wage.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could take her double-charge checks and Saturday premium together.
whatWouldHelp: A **posted paid role**, after-cost mortgage-covering hours, paid trial and signed offer would help.
